title: Treasure Island
author: Robert Louis Stevenson
ru: Юный Джим Хокинс, карта сокровищ, пираты и одноногий Джон Сильвер

chapters.title: Chapter 1. The Old Sea-Dog at the Admiral Benbow
chapters.text:
Squire Trelawney, Dr Livesey and the other gentlemen have asked me to write down the whole story of Treasure Island. They want me to keep nothing back except the position of the island, because there is still treasure there. So I take up my pen and go back to the time when my father kept the Admiral Benbow inn and the old sea-dog first came to stay under our roof.

I remember him as if it were yesterday. He came slowly up to the door, and a man pushed his sea chest behind him in a wheelbarrow. He was tall, strong and heavy, with skin burned brown by the sun. Across one cheek there was a dirty white scar from a sword. He looked around our little bay, whistling, and then he broke into the old sea song that he sang so often afterwards:

“Fifteen men on the dead man's chest — Yo-ho-ho, and a bottle of rum!”

“This is a handy little bay,” he said. “Do you get much company here, mate?”

My father told him no, very little, sorry to say.

“Well then, this is the place for me.” He threw three or four gold coins on the table. “Tell me when I've drunk my way through that. And you can call me captain.”

He was a silent man. All day he walked along the cliffs with a brass telescope. All evening he sat in the corner by the fire and drank strong rum and water. Every day he asked if any sailors had passed by on the road. At first we thought he wanted company. Then we understood: he wanted to avoid them.

One day he took me aside. “Jim,” he said, “keep your eyes open for a sailor with one leg, and tell me the moment he appears. I'll pay you a silver coin on the first of every month.”

How that man haunted my dreams! On stormy nights, when the wind shook the house, I saw him in a thousand forms. Sometimes he was a monster with only one leg, right in the middle of his body. He jumped over hedges and ditches after me, and I could never run fast enough.

The captain frightened our guests too. When he drank too much, he sang his wicked old songs and made everybody sing with him. He told terrible stories about storms and hangings and men who walked the plank. But I think the young men from the village secretly liked him. “A real old sea-dog,” they called him.

Only one man ever stood up to him. My father was very ill that winter, and one evening Dr Livesey came to see him. While the doctor was talking quietly to a friend, the captain hit the table with his fist.

“Silence there!” he shouted.

“Were you speaking to me, sir?” asked the doctor.

The captain swore and pulled out a long sailor's knife. The doctor didn't even move.

“If you don't put that knife away this minute,” he said calmly, “I promise you will hang for it.”

For a moment the two men stared at each other. Then the captain put the knife away and sat down, growling like a beaten dog.

Soon after that, on a cold January morning, a pale stranger came into the inn. Two fingers were missing from his left hand.

“Is my mate Bill here?” he asked with an ugly smile. “He has a scar on one cheek.”

The captain was out on the cliffs, so the stranger waited behind the door like a cat waiting for a mouse.

“Bill,” he said softly, when the captain came in.

The captain turned round, and all the brown went out of his face. He looked as if he had seen a ghost.

“Black Dog!” he said.

They sent me out of the room. For a while I heard only low, angry voices. Then there was a crash and a cry, and two swords flashed. Black Dog ran out of the door with blood pouring from his shoulder and disappeared down the road.

The captain stood looking after him. Then he put his hand to his head, swayed — and fell to the floor like a stone.

chapters.title: Chapter 2. The Black Spot and the Map
chapters.text:
“It's a stroke,” said Dr Livesey, kneeling beside the captain. “I warned him about the rum. One more glass, and it will kill him.”

The captain lived, but he was weak and frightened now. That evening he called me to his bed.

“Jim,” he whispered, “it's my sea chest they want. I sailed with Captain Flint, the worst pirate who ever lived. I was his first mate, and I'm the only one who knows the place. If they give me the black spot, you ride to that doctor and tell him to bring soldiers.”

“But what is the black spot, captain?”

“It's a pirate's message, mate. It means: your time is up.”

That same night my poor father died.

After the funeral, I was standing at the door when I heard a tap-tap-tapping on the frozen road. A blind man was coming towards the inn, feeling his way with his stick. He wore an old sea cloak with a hood. I never saw a more horrible figure in my life.

“Will any kind friend tell a poor blind man where he is?” he called in a strange, sing-song voice.

“You are at the Admiral Benbow, my good man,” I said.

I held out my hand to help him, and he took it in a grip like iron.

“Now, boy,” he said in a very different voice, “take me to the captain, or I'll break your arm.”

I led him in. When the captain saw us, terror filled his face. The blind man pressed something into his hand, then let go of me and tapped out of the door with surprising speed.

The captain looked at the paper.

“Ten o'clock!” he cried. “Six hours. We'll beat them yet!” He jumped to his feet, made a strange sound in his throat and fell flat on his face. He was dead.

It was the black spot. On the back someone had written: “You have till ten tonight.”

My mother and I ran to the village for help, but when the men heard the name of Captain Flint, they went white. Only one young man agreed to ride to Dr Livesey. So we went back to the dark inn alone, because my mother wanted the money the captain owed us.

I found the key on a string round the dead man's neck. In the chest there was a packet wrapped in oilcloth and a bag of gold coins from many countries. My mother began to count out exactly what we were owed — not a penny more. Then, in the frosty silence, I heard it: tap-tap-tap on the road.

“Run, Mother!” I said. I grabbed the packet, and we ran out into the darkness.

My mother fainted near the bridge, and I pulled her under it just in time. Seven or eight men ran past. I heard the door crash open and then a shout: “Bill's dead!”

“Search him, you lazy dogs!” cried the blind man. “Is the paper there?”

“The money's there. But Flint's papers are gone!”

“It's that boy! Find him!”

But then we heard horses on the road — customs officers, who hunted smugglers. The pirates ran in every direction. The blind man was left alone. “Don't leave me, mates!” he screamed. “Don't leave old Pew!” He ran this way and that, and fell right under the horses. He never moved again.

The officers carried my mother safely to the village, and that same night I took the packet to Squire Trelawney's house, where the doctor was having dinner. The Squire was a tall, red-faced gentleman who never stopped talking.

We opened the packet together. Inside was a map of an island, with a hill called Spy-glass and three red crosses. Beside one cross, someone had written: “Bulk of treasure here.”

“Flint's treasure!” cried the Squire. “Livesey, I'm going to Bristol tomorrow. In three weeks I'll have the best ship in England. Hawkins will come as cabin boy, and you'll be the ship's doctor!”

“Trelawney,” said the doctor, “there's only one man I'm afraid of.”

“Who is that? Name the dog, sir!”

“You,” said the doctor. “You can't hold your tongue.”

He was right. But none of us knew yet how many men would die for that piece of paper.

chapters.title: Chapter 3. Long John Silver
chapters.text:
It took longer than three weeks. While the Squire was in Bristol, I stayed at the Squire's house with old Redruth, his gamekeeper. I studied the map for hours and dreamed of the island. But I never dreamed of anything as strange as our real adventures.

At last a letter came from the Squire.

“I have bought a fine ship, the Hispaniola,” he wrote. “And I have found a wonderful man — an old sailor with one leg who keeps a pub here. He wants to go to sea again as ship's cook. His name is Long John Silver, and he has helped me find a crew of tough old sailors in just a few days.”

A sailor with one leg! I felt a small, cold fear. But I was too excited to think about it for long. I said goodbye to my mother and travelled to Bristol with Redruth.

The harbour was full of ships from every corner of the world. Sailors with rings in their ears sang as they worked, and the air smelled of tar and salt. The Squire sent me at once with a note to Silver's pub, the Spy-glass.

I knew Silver the moment I saw him. His left leg was cut off near the hip, and he carried a wooden crutch under his arm. But he moved on it like a bird, hopping between the tables with wonderful speed. He had a face as big as a ham, and he was whistling and joking with every customer.

Could this be the one-legged sailor the captain was afraid of? Surely not. He looked far too honest and friendly.

“So you're our new cabin boy!” he said, and shook my hand warmly.

Just then a man in the corner got up and hurried out. I knew that pale face at once.

“Stop him!” I cried. “It's Black Dog!”

“I don't care who he is,” shouted Silver, “he hasn't paid! Harry, run and catch him!” Then he turned to me. “Black Dog, you say? Never heard of him. Though I think he came in here once with a blind beggar.”

“That was Pew,” I said. “He was a pirate too.”

“A pirate! In my house!” Silver looked shocked. Then he shook his head sadly. “And what will the Squire think of me now, Jim? Pirates drinking my rum!”

He seemed so honest and so upset that I believed every word. Later I understood what a fine actor he was.

The captain of the Hispaniola, Captain Smollett, was a different kind of man — sharp, serious and never pleased.

“I don't like this voyage,” he told the Squire. “I don't like the men, and I don't like my first mate. Every sailor on board knows we are going to find treasure. Somebody has talked too much. That's dangerous, sir.”

On the captain's orders, the guns and gunpowder were moved to the back of the ship, near our cabins, and the Squire's own men — Redruth, Hunter and Joyce — slept there too.

We sailed at dawn. On the voyage, Silver was the most popular man on board. The sailors called him Barbecue. In a cage in his kitchen lived his green parrot.

“I call her Captain Flint, after the famous pirate,” Silver told me. “She's maybe two hundred years old, Jim. She's seen more wickedness than the devil himself.”

“Pieces of eight! Pieces of eight!” screamed the parrot. Pieces of eight were old Spanish silver coins — the money every pirate dreamed of.

Only the first mate, Mr Arrow, gave us trouble. He was often drunk, and one dark, stormy night he simply disappeared. “He fell overboard,” said the men.

On the last evening before we reached the island, I wanted an apple. There was a big barrel of apples on deck, with only a few left at the bottom, so I climbed right inside. It was warm and dark in there, and the rocking of the ship made me sleepy.

Then somebody heavy sat down against the barrel, and I heard Silver's voice.

Before he had said a dozen words, I was wide awake and shaking. The lives of all the honest men on board now depended on me alone.

chapters.title: Chapter 4. What I Heard in the Apple Barrel
chapters.text:
“No, not me,” Silver was saying. “Flint was the captain. I was his right-hand man. I lost my leg in the same battle where old Pew lost his eyes. Even Flint was afraid of me. Afraid of me, and proud of it.”

“Most pirates are fools,” Silver went on in a soft, friendly voice. “They spend everything on rum and end up as beggars. Not me. My money's safe in banks all over England, my wife is selling the pub, and when this voyage is over, I'll live like a gentleman. Now, Dick, are you with us?”

“I'm with you, John,” said Dick. “Here's my hand on it.”

So most of our sailors were Flint's old pirates, and Silver was their leader! Then Israel Hands, the man who steered the ship, came and sat with them.

“How much longer, Barbecue?” he asked.

“Until the very last moment,” said Silver sharply. “Smollett can sail the ship. The Squire and the doctor have the map. Let them find the treasure and help us carry it on board. Then we'll finish them off.”

“And what do we do with them then?” asked Dick.

“Dead men don't bite,” said Silver. “That's what I say. But the Squire is mine. I'll twist his head off with these hands.” Then his voice became warm again. “Dick, be a good lad and get me an apple from that barrel.”

I can't describe my terror. I heard Dick get up. In a moment his hand would come down into the barrel and find me. But Hands stopped him.

“Forget the apples,” he said. “Let's have some rum.”

Dick went off for the rum, and at that moment a cry came from above.

“Land ho!”

I slipped out of the barrel and joined the others on deck. In the moonlight we could see three hills, the highest with its top in the clouds. It was exactly like the map.

“I know this island,” said Silver. “That big hill is the Spy-glass.” Then he put his hand on my shoulder. “Ah, you'll love this island, Jim. You can climb the hills like a goat!”

I almost screamed when he touched me.

As soon as I could, I told the captain, the Squire and the doctor everything.

“Captain Smollett, you were right and I was wrong,” said the Squire, red in the face.

We counted the honest men: the captain, the Squire, the doctor, Redruth, Hunter, Joyce and me. Seven of us — and one of the seven was a boy — against nineteen. We couldn't turn back, or the pirates would attack at once. We had to wait.

The next morning we anchored near the island. It was a grey, sad place, covered in dark woods, and the air smelled of rotten leaves. The men were angry, and a mutiny — a rebellion against the captain — could start at any moment. So the captain gave them the afternoon on shore.

Thirteen men went, with Silver in charge. And then I did something crazy. I jumped into one of the boats too.

As soon as my boat touched the beach, I ran into the woods. I was free! Then I heard voices. I hid behind a bush and saw Silver with Tom, one of the honest sailors.

“Tom, join us,” Silver was saying. “It's your only chance.”

Suddenly a long, terrible scream came from far away.

“What was that?” cried Tom.

“That?” said Silver, smiling. “That was probably Alan.”

“Alan! Then you've killed him, John Silver. Well, kill me too if you can. I won't join you.”

Tom turned and walked away. Silver threw his crutch, and it hit Tom hard in the back. Tom fell, and in a second Silver was on top of him with a knife.

The world went round and round in front of my eyes. When I came to my senses, Silver was blowing a whistle to call his men.

I ran and ran, I didn't care where. Then something dark and hairy jumped from among the trees and hid behind a trunk. Was it a man or an animal? Now there were enemies in front of me as well as behind.

chapters.title: Chapter 5. The Man of the Island and the Stockade
chapters.text:
The creature came out from behind the tree. It was a man — but what a man! His face was burned black by the sun, and he was dressed in old pieces of sail and goat skins. He fell on his knees in front of me.

“Who are you?” I asked.

“Ben Gunn,” he answered, in a rusty voice, like a lock that nobody had opened for years. “I'm poor Ben Gunn, I am. And I haven't spoken to another man for three years.”

“Were you shipwrecked?”

“No, mate — marooned. Left alone on the island as a punishment.” He looked at me hungrily. “You don't happen to have a piece of cheese on you, do you? No? Many a long night I've dreamed of cheese — toasted cheese, mostly — and woken up still here.”

Years before, he told me, he had sailed with Captain Flint. Flint came to this island with six sailors to bury his treasure. A week later he came back to the ship alone. The six men were dead, and only Flint knew where the gold was.

“Three years ago I came back here on another ship,” said Ben Gunn. “We looked for Flint's treasure for twelve days and found nothing. So they left me here with a gun and a spade. ‘You can find the money yourself, Ben Gunn,’ they said.” He winked at me. “And now I'm rich, Jim. Rich! You tell your Squire that.”

Was he mad? Before I could decide, a cannon shot thundered across the island. Through the trees I saw a flag flying — the British flag.

“Those are your friends,” said Ben Gunn. “Silver would fly the Jolly Roger — the black flag of the pirates. They're in Flint's old stockade. If you need me, I'll be near the white rock. I've got a boat there.”

Later the doctor told me what had happened. Our men had loaded a small boat with guns and food and left the ship for the stockade — a strong log house on a hill, with a spring and a high wooden fence. One honest sailor, Abraham Gray, came with them. The pirates fired the ship's cannon at them, the boat sank near the beach, and most of the food was lost. Then the pirates attacked in the woods, and poor old Redruth was shot dead.

When the shooting stopped, I ran towards the flag and climbed over the fence. My friends welcomed me with joy. But we had very little food.

The next morning Silver came with a white flag.

“Cap'n Smollett,” he said politely, “give us the map, and I'll put you all safe on shore somewhere.”

The captain looked at him coldly.

“Listen to me, my man. You can't find the treasure. You can't sail the ship. Give up your weapons, and I'll take you home to a fair trial. If not, the next time I see you I'll put a bullet in your back.”

Silver's face went dark with anger. He had been sitting on the sand, and nobody would help him up. Someone in the house laughed. So he crawled to the fence, pulled himself up on his crutch and spat on the ground.

“Laugh, by thunder, laugh!” he shouted. “Before an hour's out, I'll break your old log house like a rum barrel. And those of you who die will be the lucky ones!”

He kept his word. The pirates attacked from three sides. They climbed the fence, shouting and firing. For a few minutes there was smoke and screaming everywhere. I grabbed a sword and ran outside, and a pirate's blade passed right over my head. Then it was over. The pirates were running back into the woods, and five of them lay dead.

But we had paid for it. Joyce and Hunter were dead, and the captain was badly wounded.

That afternoon the doctor took the map and a pistol and walked off into the woods. I guessed he was going to find Ben Gunn. The house was hot and smelled of blood, and I was jealous of the doctor.

So I filled my pockets with biscuits, took two pistols, and climbed over the fence when nobody was watching. It was a mad thing to do. But I was a boy, and I had made up my mind.

chapters.title: Chapter 6. My Sea Adventure
chapters.text:
By sunset I had found Ben Gunn's boat under some goat skins by the white rock. It was a tiny round thing of skins on a wooden frame, like something a child had made. But it floated.

I had a new plan: to paddle out in the dark and cut the Hispaniola's anchor rope. Without a ship, the pirates would be lost.

On the beach the pirates were singing around a big fire. The little boat was terrible to steer — it turned round and round in every direction except the one I wanted. But at last the tide carried me to the side of the ship.

With my knife I cut the thick rope, little by little, until it finally broke and the Hispaniola began to move.

Through the cabin window I heard two drunk men fighting — Israel Hands and another pirate, O'Brien.

My boat was pulled along with the ship towards the open sea. I lay down in the bottom and waited to die. Somehow I fell asleep.

I woke up in bright daylight, drifting along the coast, and great waves were thundering on the rocks. Not far away was the Hispaniola, sailing wildly in circles. Nobody was steering her.

Then a wave lifted me, and I jumped and caught the side of the ship just as she crashed down and sank my little boat.

On the deck O'Brien lay dead. Israel Hands was sitting against the side of the ship, pale and wounded.

“Brandy,” he groaned.

I gave him some. Then I said, “Mr Hands, I've come on board to take possession of this ship. From now on, I'm your captain.”

I pulled down the pirate flag and threw it overboard. “God save the King!” I said. “And that's the end of Captain Silver.”

“You can't sail her alone, Cap'n Hawkins,” said Hands with a sly look. “But I'll tell you how, if you give me food and drink.”

With help from Hands, I began to sail round the island to a quiet inlet in the north. I was proud of myself. But I didn't trust Hands for a moment.

“Go down and bring me some wine, Jim,” he said. “This brandy is too strong for my head.”

I went below, then crept back and watched. Hands crawled quickly across the deck, took a long knife from a pile of ropes, and hid it in his jacket.

I came back with the wine as if I had seen nothing. Soon the ship ran gently onto the sand. I was so busy watching the shore that I forgot about Hands. Then something made me turn — perhaps a sound, perhaps a shadow. He was coming at me with the knife in his hand.

I climbed the mast like a monkey, as high as I could. There I quickly loaded my pistols again, because the sea water had made them useless.

Hands began to climb after me, slowly, with the knife between his teeth.

“One more step, Mr Hands,” I said, “and I'll blow your brains out! Dead men don't bite, you know.”

He stopped and took the knife out of his mouth.

“Jim,” he said, “I think we'll have to make peace, you and me—”

Suddenly his arm moved. Something flew through the air, and I felt a sharp pain. The knife had pinned my shoulder to the mast. In that moment of shock, both my pistols went off. With a cry, Hands fell into the sea.

Through the clear water I saw him lying on the sandy bottom, with little fish swimming over him. He never came up again.

At last I pulled myself free. The wound was not deep. I climbed down, waded to the shore through the shallow water and set off across the island.

It was night when I reached the stockade. A red fire was burning low inside it. That was strange — the captain never allowed a fire at night. I crept in through the door and stepped over a sleeping man.

Then a sharp voice screamed out of the darkness:

“Pieces of eight! Pieces of eight! Pieces of eight!”

It was Captain Flint, Silver's parrot. A man woke with a shout, and someone came in with a burning torch.

I was in the hands of the pirates.

chapters.title: Chapter 7. Prisoner of the Pirates
chapters.text:
In the torchlight I saw six pirates and no sign of my friends.

“Well, well, here's Jim Hawkins!” said Silver cheerfully. “Just dropped in to see us, eh?”

He sat down on a barrel and filled his pipe.

“Where are my friends?” I asked.

“Yesterday morning the doctor came with a white flag,” said Silver. “‘Cap'n Silver,’ he says, ‘you're sold out. The ship's gone.’ And so she was. So we made a deal. They left the stockade, and we got the house, the food and the brandy.”

So I was alone. Then I did something brave, or perhaps something foolish.

“I know I'll probably die,” I said, my voice shaking. “But first, listen. It was I who hid in the apple barrel and heard all your plans. It was I who cut the ship's rope, I who killed Israel Hands, and I who hid her where you'll never find her. Kill me if you like. But if you let me live, I'll speak for you in court and save you from hanging.”

An old pirate called Morgan pulled out his knife.

“Let's finish him!” he shouted.

“Stop!” cried Silver. “Do you think you're the captain here, Tom Morgan? Anyone who wants to fight me, take out your knife. I'll see the colour of his blood before this pipe is empty.”

Nobody moved. But soon the pirates went outside to whisper together.

“They're going to get rid of me, Jim,” said Silver quietly. “You're my last card, and I'm yours. I'll save your life from them, and you save me from hanging.”

They came back and pushed a small round piece of paper into Silver's hand. The black spot! It was cut from a page of the Bible.

“You've ruined this voyage, John Silver,” said one of them. “And you're protecting this boy.”

Silver laughed. “Ruined it, have I? Then look at this!” And he threw a piece of paper on the floor.

It was the map with the three red crosses! Why had the doctor given it to him? The pirates jumped on it like cats on a mouse. In a minute they had forgotten the black spot and Silver was their captain again.

In the morning the doctor came to look after the sick pirates, as calmly as if he were visiting patients at home. He asked to talk to me alone, by the fence.

“Jim,” he said, “you ran away when the captain was too ill to stop you. That was a cowardly thing to do. But now — jump over the fence and run, and we'll run together!”

“No,” I said. “I gave Silver my word.” And I told him where the ship was.

“Jim, at every step of this adventure, it's you who saves our lives,” he said. Then he turned to Silver. “A piece of advice, Silver: when you find that treasure, watch out for trouble.”

After breakfast we set out for the gold. Silver had tied a rope round my waist, and he held the other end, like a man with a dog.

Under a tall pine tree, one of them screamed. A human skeleton was lying on the ground, its long arms pointing straight above its head.

“One of Flint's jokes,” said Silver. “He killed this man and laid him here to point the way.”

Then, from the trees ahead, a high, thin voice began to sing:

“Fifteen men on the dead man's chest — Yo-ho-ho, and a bottle of rum!”

The men went white. Then the voice called out: “Darby McGraw! Bring the rum, Darby!”

“Those were Flint's last words!” cried one man. “It's Flint's ghost!”

But Silver did not give up. “Who ever heard of a ghost with an echo?” he said. “I know that voice. It's Ben Gunn's!”

“Ben Gunn!” said Morgan. “Nobody's afraid of Ben Gunn — alive or dead.”

The pirates hurried on, pulling me behind them.

Then the first men stopped with a low cry.

In front of us was a great hole. It was not new — grass was growing at the bottom, among some old boards. On one of them was written “Walrus” — the name of Flint's ship.

The treasure was gone.

chapters.title: Chapter 8. The Treasure
chapters.text:
Silver understood first. Before the others had stopped staring, he had changed sides again. He quietly passed me a pistol.

“Get ready, Jim,” he whispered. “Here comes trouble.”

The pirates jumped into the hole and dug with their hands. George Merry found a single coin and held it up.

“Two guineas!” he roared. “Is this your treasure, John Silver? You knew it was gone all along!”

“Keep digging, boys,” said Silver coolly. “Maybe you'll find some peanuts.”

The pirates climbed out on the other side. Now the hole was between us — Silver and me on one side, five angry men on the other.

“Mates,” shouted Merry, “there's just two of them — an old cripple and a boy. Now, boys—”

He raised his arm to lead the attack. But at that moment — crack! crack! crack! — three shots came out of the bushes. Merry fell head first into the hole, another man fell beside him, and the other three turned and ran for their lives.

Out of the trees came the doctor, Abraham Gray and Ben Gunn, with smoking guns.

“Thank you kindly, doctor,” said Silver, wiping his face. “You came just in time for me and Hawkins. And so it's you, Ben Gunn! Well, well.”

“I'm Ben Gunn, I am,” said Ben shyly. “And how do you do, Mr Silver?”

Now everything became clear. In his lonely years on the island, Ben Gunn had found the treasure and carried it, little by little, to his cave. When the doctor heard this, he knew the map was useless. So he gave it to Silver and moved our people to the cave.

“But I couldn't let them kill you, Jim,” said the doctor. “Ben ran ahead, and his singing slowed the pirates down.”

We took one of the pirates' boats round to the north inlet, where the Hispaniola was floating quietly on the high tide. Then we rowed back to the beach below Ben Gunn's cave.

In the cave the Squire was waiting for us, and Captain Smollett was lying by a fire. Behind them, in the shadows, lay great piles of gold.

“John Silver,” said the Squire, “you are a terrible villain. I've been told not to take you to court, and I won't. But the dead men hang around your neck like stones.”

“Thank you kindly, sir,” said Silver, and he saluted.

“Is that you, John Silver?” said the captain. “What are you doing here, man?”

“I've come back to my duty, sir,” said Silver.

“Ah!” said the captain, and that was all.

What a supper that was, with all my friends around me! And there was Silver, sitting a little behind us, eating happily, as polite as ever.

For the next few days we carried the treasure to the ship. There were English, French, Spanish and Portuguese coins, and others from countries I didn't know — round ones, square ones, and ones with holes in the middle.

We left the three pirates who were still alive on the island, with food, gunpowder and tools. As we sailed away, they knelt on the sand and begged us to take them.

On the way home we stopped at a port in Spanish America to find more sailors. There, one night, Silver escaped in a small boat with a bag of gold coins. I think we were all glad to lose him so cheaply.

We reached Bristol at last, and everybody got a share of the treasure. Gray saved his money and now owns part of a fine ship. Ben Gunn got a thousand pounds and spent it all in nineteen days. Now he works for the Squire and sings in church on Sundays.

Of Silver we have heard nothing. Perhaps he found his wife and lives somewhere in comfort with her and Captain Flint. I almost hope so — because his chances of comfort in the next world are very small.

We never went back for Flint's bars of silver, and they are still lying where he buried them. But nothing will ever take me back to that terrible island. The worst dreams I ever have are when I hear the waves crashing on its coast, or when I sit up in bed with the parrot's sharp voice still ringing in my ears:

“Pieces of eight! Pieces of eight!”
